claims.claim: Roy C. Lackey treats a physical detail that does not belong in its setting — cart tracks on a beach — as the load-bearing evidence linking two scenes.
claims.source: Roy C. Lackey, Urth mailing list, 10 September 2006
claims.quote: had no business being on that beach.
claims.page: message body, reply on the Sand Garden

verdicts.trueWording: "If this is so, Wolfe is an amazing teacher: he shows Severian instructing us on the power of symbols yet simultaneously being blind to them (making their power all the more evident)." The tomb limb is carried by the same message: "Does Severian see the connection between the symbols graven on his tomb and what he would later do?" and "Severian was shaped by the tomb that bore his face".
verdicts.note: Raw page reached via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20210416053620id_/http://lists.urth.net/pipermail/urth-urth.net/2006-September/003004.html (live host refuses connections: ECONNREFUSED 69.163.136.55:443, and a browser-UA curl timed out). Byline and date on the page: Bruce Hayles, brucehayles at gmail.com, Sun Sep 10 09:46:58 PDT 2006. Quote appears word for word (it spans a line wrap in the raw source: "...instructing us on the / power of symbols"). Every limb holds: the rule ("It seems instead that Wolfe is giving us a rule"; the quoted symbol speech "We believe that we invent symbols. The truth is that they invent us..."), Severian as its stater ("he gives us the symbol speech"), and the blindness to the tomb's symbols — the fountain, ship volant and rose Hayles calls "the symbols graven on his tomb".

verdicts.trueWording: "...we can use that rule to derive the influence of the ship volant, the fountain, and the rose, despite the fact that Severian does not emphasize them whatsoever."
verdicts.note: Same raw Wayback capture of 003004. Quote appears word for word. Three symbols named (ship volant, fountain, rose); the narrator who does not emphasise them is Severian; "importance" is the message's own frame ("It certainly seems Wolfe is at least trying to tell us they are important"). One wording nuance short of an unsupported limb: Hayles writes "we CAN use that rule to derive", where the claim says the reader "must" derive — the modality is softer on the page, but the operation, the three symbols and the absence of emphasis are all stated as claimed.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the cart tracks are the load-bearing evidence for the link — Lackey offers them as one corroborating detail among several ("right down to the tracks"), alongside the person to be met being Severian's future self and the concealed woman being Thecla, and he hedges the whole parallel as holding "to some extent".
verdicts.trueWording: "...the Sand Garden to some extent replicated/foreshadowed what would happen months later on the beach, right down to the tracks of the two-wheeled cart, which had no business being on that beach."
verdicts.note: Raw page reached via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20210416053700id_/http://lists.urth.net/pipermail/urth-urth.net/2006-September/003007.html (live host down as above). Byline and date on the page: Roy C. Lackey, rclackey at stic.net, Sun Sep 10 23:43:34 PDT 2006. The quote "had no business being on that beach." is on the page word for word, and the out-of-place-physical-detail limb (two-wheeled cart tracks on a beach) is fully supported. What the page does not support is the weight the claim assigns it: the tracks are the sharpest concrete correspondence in a list of correspondences, not stated to be the evidence the link rests on.
